The fastest way to spread adoption is to make dedicated infrastructure investments before broad access. A small team—sometimes even a single person—connects the tool to developer workflows before developers first touch it. At one company, a few engineers built a set of plugins and MCPs that were available on day one. At another, an entire team focused on managing AI coding tools built the infrastructure before rollout began. In both cases, the first developer experience was productive rather than frustrating, and adoption spread from there. Teams doing this work today often sit under Developer Experience or Developer Productivity, the function typically responsible for onboarding new engineers and building developer tools. In a few organizations, an emerging role is the agent manager: a hybrid PM/engineer role dedicated to managing the Claude Code ecosystem. For organizations without a dedicated team, the minimal viable version is a DRI: one person with ownership and decision rights over Claude Code configuration, permission policies, plugin marketplace, and CLAUDE.md conventions, responsible for keeping them current. Bottom-up adoption generates enthusiasm but fragments without centralization. You need a person or team to curate and promote the right Claude Code conventions, such as a standardized CLAUDE.md hierarchy or a curated set of skills and plugins. Without this work, knowledge stays tribal and adoption stalls. In large organizations, especially in regulated industries, governance questions arise early: who controls which skills and plugins are available, how do you prevent thousands of engineers from independently rebuilding the same things, and how do you ensure AI-generated code goes through the same review process as human-generated code? To address these early, we recommend starting with a defined set of approved skills, required code review processes, and limited initial access, then expanding as confidence builds.
